paras: The lynching of Jerry Smith was the hanging of a Black man by a group of men at Tiptonville, Lake county, Tennessee, in April 1888, while he was being held in jail on an accusation of attempted rape. Smith was taken from jail on the morning his case was to come before the court and was found hanging from a tree near the river bank. A Memphis wire carried the news across the country in two lines, and no one was identified as taking part.

According to the Memphis Appeal, the authorities were told on the Saturday before that Smith, 'a colored man,' had attempted to rape a white girl of about twelve, the daughter of a farmer living about three miles from Tiptonville. A constable chased him through the overflowed river bottoms, where the Appeal said both men nearly drowned, then captured him and placed him in jail.

Wednesday was court day at Tiptonville, and Smith was to be tried. Instead, in the Appeal's words, 'Judge Lynch arrived in town just before daybreak' and 'tried, convicted and executed the culprit before the legitimate tribunal was called to order.' The Memphis wire described those who took him from jail as 'a mob of farmers' or 'a crowd of farmers' and gave no number. His body was seen the following morning about a quarter of a mile back from the river bank, suspended from a tree.

The Appeal reported that the lynchers' work was done 'without leaving a trace of their identity.' No report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. About a week later the Hickman Courier noted that the Headlight, a new paper at Tiptonville, gave 'an account of the hanging of James Abernathy, colored, charged with rape,' without saying whether this was the same case.

The Memphis Appeal printed the fullest account on April 13 under the headline 'A Fiend Strangled. Summary Punishment of a Negro Rapist at Tiptonville.' It called Smith a 'brutal negro fiend,' a 'scoundrel' and 'the lascivious negro,' treated the accusation as proven and described the hanging in the mock-judicial language of 'Judge Lynch' and his 'impromptu' court. The same day a two-line Memphis dispatch ran in Washington, Ohio and Texas papers, stating as fact that Smith had 'attempted to assault a white girl.'

Copy editors gave the dispatch light or plain headings: 'Judge Lynch Officiated' in the Washington Critic, 'A Surprise Party' in the Springfield Daily Republic, 'Lynched for Rape' in the San Antonio Daily Light and 'Lynching in Tennessee' in the Richmond Dispatch. A separate condensed telegram, printed in Wheeling and later in Canton and Stanford, Kentucky, placed the lynching at Tiptonville, which the Wheeling and Canton papers located in 'Ky.', and hardened the charge to 'ruining' or 'raping' a girl of twelve. The Daily Kennebec Journal likewise said Smith was lynched 'for committing rape.'

Weekly news summaries in Arkansas, Mississippi and Tennessee papers between April 19 and 21 turned the Memphis dateline into the place of the jail, reporting that farmers took Smith 'out of the Memphis (Tenn.) jail' on the 13th. The story was still running as filler in Sheridan, Wyoming, on May 5, where the assault itself was placed 'at Memphis.' None of these papers questioned the accusation or criticized the lynching.

Reports differ on the date: the Appeal and the Wheeling telegram give Wednesday morning, April 11, while the Memphis wire, dated April 13, says 'yesterday,' the Kennebec Journal says Thursday night and the Indiana State Sentinel says 'last Friday.' The Appeal, the nearest and fullest source, also says word reached Memphis on Thursday, which may explain the wire's later date. The name James Abernathy in the Tiptonville Headlight note cannot be matched to Smith from the coverage.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'A Fiend Strangled' and called Smith a 'brutal negro fiend' and 'the lascivious negro', treating the accusation as fact and the hanging as 'summary punishment'.
Most papers ran the two-line Memphis wire under light headings such as 'A Surprise Party' and 'Judge Lynch Officiated', stating the accusation as fact without comment.
Condensed-news columns gave one line, shifting the charge from attempt to 'ruining' or 'raping'.

conflicts.note: The Appeal, the local source, says the hanging was Wednesday morning and that word reached Memphis 'yesterday' (Thursday); the wire's 'yesterday' likely reflects when the news arrived, and the later dates follow the wire dateline.
Memphis is the wire dateline; the Appeal places the jail, court and hanging at Tiptonville in Lake county.
The fullest report, the Appeal's, says attempt; the condensed briefs harden it.
